newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INSTANT VIEW - NZ CPI prompts market-led easing.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - NZ CPI prompts market-led easing.

text.p: New Zealand's consumer price index rose 0.6 percent in the September quarter and 2.4 percent for the year versus economists' consensus forecasts of 0.86 percent and 2.7 percent respectively.
Following is a selection of economists' reactions:
ADRIAN ORR, Chief Economist, National Bank:

"It's letting the market do a bit of the easing without the Reserve Bank having to say much at all. What's it's starting to do is bring the possibility of an official endorsement of an easing in December - which was the market's view originally - it's now bringing that well into odds-on. Over the months prior to this it was looking much more uncertain, with such things as general price pressure, wage pressure, poor productivity performances suggesting that even December was becoming less likely for an easing. This puts it firmly back in the camp again."
JOSELYN STROOMBERGEN, Westpac economist
Stroombergen estimated 90-day bank bills would rally 50-75 basis points.
"We could easily see 90-days under 9.5 percent, depending how the currency holds up."

Asked whether the Reserve Bank could ease its daily cash target, she said: "We could even see the Reserve Bank move in that area now. They may just want to see what the market does over the next couple of days.
"In their September economic forecasts they said they were looking for conclusive evidence (of inflation pressures easing), I think we are starting to get the first hints now."
She said there were a couple of qualifications with the number, including labour costs, rising core food prices, rents, petrol prices and insurance.
"Overall it's an excellent figure."
STEPHEN TOPLIS, economist with Doyle Paterson Brown.

"The underlying number is going to be around half of what the Reserve Bank predicted. The Reserve Bank were predicting around 0.7. We know ex-credit charges are 0.4, it's probably going to be marginally below 0.4 (quarterly underlying inflation) -- 0.35 percent or something like that.
"There's no two ways the market will rally. It's hard to know to what extent.
"This will make the Reserve Bank a little bit more comfortable -- a little, not a lot. It will take the pressure of the short-end which is looking for a catalyst to rally anyway."
Toplis said the Reserve Bank will be relieved. He said when a central bank is forecasting a high inflation rate it is nervous that the actual rate will come out above the forecast rate.
DAVID DRAGE, Treasury economist, ANZ Bank

"Obviously somewhat weaker than expected...Probably the main area of surprise was the housing group, which was certainly much weaker than expected. We would probably note, though, that the evidence of a pickup in housing activity more recently with the falls in fixed mortage rates, would perhaps introduce an element of caution there.
"Probably the other thing that surprised us somewhat was that insurance premiums and rates hadn't come through to the extent we expected. Obviously they'll be to go yet in the December quarter."
He said the data did not bring the prospect of a formal easing any closer at this stage.
"No, not at this stage. There's certainly still some areas of concern at the moment."
PETER CAVANAUGH, ASSOCIATE DIRECTOR, BANCORP

"We're seeing a market-led easing...A formal easing probably won't be likely until the (Reserve Bank's) December Monetary Policy Statement but that doesn't preclude a tacit acceptance of a market-led easing."

Cavanaugh said the market's response reflected both the lower than expected inflation data and prospects that coalition talks after Saturday's inconclusive general election could lead to a widening of the RBNZ's 0-2 percent underlying inflation target.
"Basically, the market's just pre-empting lower inflation and a potential change in policy."
On currency implications:

"Once interest rates are perceived to be at or near the bottom, then the currency will start coming off, of course. (But) whilst the bills and bonds are rallying, they will still attract capital inflows, so at this stage the currency should be stable to probably only slightly lower."
BANKERS TRUST ECONOMIST DAVID PLANK

"It was a surprisingly good number. The key question I suppose is whether it is the conclusive evidence that inflation pressures have turned the corner that the Reserve Bank was looking for and whether it feels it can ease, given the large policy uncertainty surrounding the election outcome.

"It was a positive number, it may not be enough to trigger the Reserve Bank to ease given the fiscal policy risks that are currently out there. Certainly the possibility of the Reserve Bank commenting has increased because of this number."
ROBIN CLEMENTS, chief economist, SBC Warburg New Zealand:

"Crucially, the surprise appears to have come from the housing-related side, whereas everyone was expecting quite sizeable contributions in that area. I think there's a reasonable chance that underlying inflation could be below (annual) 2.0 percent in the next quarter. And with the currency averaging about one percent higher in the September quarter than the Reserve Bank's assumption of 65 on the TWI, you could easily have inflation knocking on zero a year ahead."
"So while it will be in some sense a relief, the question is whether inflation will still fall to where the bank expects, and we don't think it will.

"So the market will probably push these bill rates down, and that can be justified because of where the TWI is. There are some people wondering whether the Reserve Bank is going to come out and officially ease, and I just think that's very unlikely.
"The Reserve Bank knows that if they come out and wave the 'go' flag when the bills are already down about 20 basis points, it's going to be a landslide.
"Monetary policy has already eased considerably from a couple of months ago anyway -- fixed rate mortgages or the market cost of borrowing money has certainly fallen."
ANTHONY BYETT, ASB ECONOMIST

"All it has done has brought forward when an easing would be possible. Instead of thinking now of the March quarter, we can probably be a bit more optimistic that we may get an easing in December. But to get one before then, I think, would be unrealistic.
"There has been a lot of tension in the market for a number of weeks, for both political and inflation reasons, and it's like a valve that has been released over the last 48 hours."
-- Wellington newsroom 64 4 473-4746
